messages.subject: plotting 3D images
parts:
Hello,

I recently noticed you added support for importing 3D datasets using some of the benchmark datasets released in GigaScience. Could you tell me the function to generate 3d images, below is the code I have tried using a benchmark dataset:

require(devtools)

dev_mode(on=T)

install_github("kbemis/Cardinal")

require(Cardinal)

setwd(".../3d_benchmark")
microbe_3d<-readImzML("Microbe_Interaction_3D_Timecourse_LP")

image(microbe_3d,feature=2000,strip=FALSE,key=FALSE,colorkey=FALSE)

Which produces a series of plots for each slice of the 3D image..I also noticed the benchmark datasets include a new coordinate space for 3D imaging: 

<userParam name="3DPositionX" value="5601.64"/>
<userParam name="3DPositionY" value="-11512.5"/>
<userParam name="3DPositionZ" value="0"/>

Is this coordinate space loaded into the ImageSet and used for 3D plotting? If so, how could I assign them in the msset? (I have my transformations parsed into R)

I have used the affine function for transforming my coordinates but often end up with many blank pixels from rotation. 

Sorry for the ton of questions..I'm very interested to do a 3D analysis in Cardinal, especially if I can use transformations I have developed elsewhere.

Heath

messages.author: 5276ff4387de2618
messages.subject: Re: plotting 3D images
parts:
Hi Heath,

For now, 3D plotting uses the image() method, but with 3 variables in the formula instead of 2 (the 'formula' argument the defaults to '~ x * y' if nothing is given).

For that dataset, try:

image(microbe, ~ x * z * y, mz=262, contrast.enhance="suppress", phi=0, theta=270)

For that dataset, the time points are confounded with the z-axis, so I would suggest redefining the coordinates, for example:

m2 <- microbe

m2$sample <- factor(sapply(m2$z, function(z) {
if ( z %in% 1:6 ) {
1
} else if ( z %in% 7:12 ) {
2
} else if ( z %in% 13:18 )  {
3
}
}), labels=c("t = 4", "t = 8", "t = 11"))

m2$z <- sapply(m2$z, function(z) {
if ( z %in% 1:6 ) {
z
} else if ( z %in% 7:12 ) {
z-6
} else if ( z %in% 13:18 )  {
z-12
}
})

m2$x <- mapply(function(x, t) {
switch(as.integer(t),
x-30,
x-15,
x)
}, m2$x, m2$sample)

varMetadata(m2)[c("x","y","z","sample"),"labelType"] <- "dim"

protocolData(m2) <- AnnotatedDataFrame(data=data.frame(row.names=sampleNames(m2)))

m2 <- regeneratePositions(m2)

validObject(m2)

Then doing:

image(m2, ~ x * z * y, mz=262, contrast.enhance="suppress", layout=c(3,1), theta=-45)

which should be a more useful visualization.

Internally, this plotting is done using persp() and points(), so check persp() documentation for additional arguments to control the 3D angle, etc.

Currently, Cardinal only uses the <userParam name="3DPositionZ"> coordinates to create the z coordinate, but then discards them. Unfortunately, as you've noticed, since Cardinal expects everything to be on a regular grid, this results in blank pixels in some places.

Right now, all of the mass spectra are loaded and included, but there will be duplicate rows in the coord(). This doesn't impact plotting (the duplicates just won't be plotted), but will be a problem for the built-in processing and analysis methods, so if you want to use any of those, I suggest doing:

microbe <- microbe[,!duplicated(coord(microbe))]

before any processing or analysis. Unfortunately, this throws away data, but I don't have a better solution at this point, given how the MSImageSet class is designed.

Valid coordinates in an MSImageSet need to be integers, but you can assign any variables such as transformed coordinates into the pixelData, simply by:

microbe$3DPositionX <- 3DPositionX # OR
pData(microbe$3DPositionX) <- 3DPositionX

and use them with any custom scripts. But for now, non-integer coordinates can't be used in plotting.

-Kyle

messages.author: 5276ff4387de2618
messages.subject: Re: plotting 3D images
parts:
Thank you for your comments, Heath!

I am not sure of one that can plot images of data from a non-regular grid. Especially if they use rasters, most designed specifically for images expect a regular grid.

However, it occurs to me that my implementation for 3D plotting doesn't rely on rasters, and with some tweaking would work for data on non-regular grid.

This is done using the trans3d() function with points() after calling persp(), to plot a cloud of points. The same can be accomplished with cloud() in lattice. The 'rgl' package also has interactive implementations. For 3D, you're not longer rastering flat images, so a lot more is possible (as the expense of much slower plotting).

-Kyle
